name: AI Safety and Scam Awareness for Seniors
objectives: Given a call, text or email, identify the four signs of a scam: pretending, a problem or prize, pressure and an unusual payment, naming every sign the message shows
When a caller sounds like a loved one in an emergency, hang up and check with your loved one or their parent on a number you already have, sending no money before you check

Given an unexpected text, email, website or pop-up, contact the company yourself by typing its real address or calling a number from your card or bill, without clicking the link or calling the number in the message
Every time a message or call worries you, use the Stop, Check, Call steps, using only a number you already trust

When an unexpected caller or message asks for information or money, refuse to give private numbers, passwords, codes or unusual payments, and call your bank if you already did, sharing nothing with an unexpected contact
After a scam or attempted scam, name where to report it and get help in the United States, naming at least two correct places

lessons.title: Lesson 1: The four signs of a scam
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Name the four signs that a call, text or email is probably a scam.
This lesson builds toward: Given a call, text or email, you will identify the four signs of a scam: pretending, a problem or prize, pressure and an unusual payment, naming every sign the message shows.
The Federal Trade Commission (FTC), the US government's consumer protection agency, describes four common signs of a scam. Learn these four and you will catch most scams, with or without AI.
1. They pretend to be someone you trust: a government office, your bank, a well-known company, a charity or a family member. 2. They say there is a problem or a prize: you owe money, your account is locked, or you won something but must pay a fee. 3. They pressure you to act now and may tell you not to hang up or not to tell anyone. 4. They want payment in an unusual way: gift cards, wire transfers, cryptocurrency, a payment app, or a check they want you to cash and send money back from.
If you see even one of these signs, slow down and check before you do anything.
Words to know:
- FTC: the Federal Trade Commission, the US government agency that protects people from scams.
- Impersonate: to pretend to be someone else.
Official sources:
- FTC: How to avoid a scam
Try it now: Take an index card or piece of paper. Write "My scam safety card" at the top, then write the four signs in your own words.
You can now name the four signs of a scam.

check.q: Which is one of the four signs of a scam?
options: A message from a number you saved yourself
A letter you were expecting
They want payment by gift card or wire transfer
A friend asking how you are
check.why: An unusual payment, like gift cards or wire transfers, is one of the four signs.

check.q: A caller says you owe taxes and must pay today or be arrested. How many signs do you see, and what do you do?
options: None; pay to be safe
Several signs: a problem and pressure; slow down and check before doing anything
One sign, so it must be real
No signs because it is the government
check.why: A problem plus pressure to act now are scam signs; even one sign means slow down and check.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: AI voice copies and fake family emergencies
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Recognize a fake emergency call that may use an AI copy of a loved one's voice.
This lesson builds toward: When a caller sounds like a loved one in an emergency, you will hang up and check with your loved one or their parent on a number you already have, sending no money before you check.
With a short recording of someone's voice, such as a video posted online, scammers can use AI to make a copy of that voice. Then they call a grandparent, crying or panicked: "Grandma, I've been in an accident, I need money for bail, please don't tell Mom."
Sometimes a second person comes on the line pretending to be a lawyer or police officer. They ask for cash, gift cards or a wire transfer, and may even send a courier to pick up money at your door.
The voice may sound real, but the four signs are still there: pretending, a problem, pressure and secrecy, and an unusual payment. Hang up and call your loved one, or their parent, on the number you already have. A family code word that only your family knows is a strong extra check.
Step by step:
- Notice the signs: panic, secrecy, a request for money.
- Hang up, even if the voice sounds real.
- Call your loved one or their parent on the number you already have.
- Ask for your family code word if you have one.
Words to know:
- Voice cloning: using AI to copy someone's voice from a short recording.
- Courier: a person sent to pick up or deliver something.
Try it now: On your safety card, write the names and phone numbers of two family members you would call to check an emergency. Then call one of them and agree on a family code word.
You can now recognize a fake family emergency call and check it safely.

check.q: How can scammers copy a loved one's voice?
options: Only by meeting them in person
They cannot
By guessing
With AI and a short recording, such as a video posted online
check.why: A short recording is enough for AI to copy a voice.

check.q: A crying voice like your granddaughter's says she needs bail and not to tell her mom. What do you do?
options: Hang up and call her or her parent on the number you already have
Send the money quickly
Keep it secret as she asks
Give the lawyer your bank number
check.why: Even if the voice sounds real, call back on a number you trust before doing anything.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Fake messages, websites and pop-ups
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Spot a fake text, email, website or pop-up warning.
This lesson builds toward: Given an unexpected text, email, website or pop-up, you will contact the company yourself by typing its real address or calling a number from your card or bill, without clicking the link or calling the number in the message. Given a call, text or email, you will identify the four signs of a scam: pretending, a problem or prize, pressure and an unusual payment, naming every sign the message shows.
AI helps scammers write texts and emails with perfect spelling that look like they come from your bank, a delivery company, Medicare or Amazon. Good spelling no longer proves a message is real.
Common tricks: "Your package could not be delivered, click here." "Unusual activity on your account, log in now." A pop-up on your computer saying it has a virus and you must call a number. These links and numbers lead to the scammer.
Do not click links or call numbers in unexpected messages. Close the message, and go to the company's real website by typing the address yourself, or call the number on the back of your card or on a bill you trust. Medicare says it will never call to sell you anything or visit your home.
Step by step:
- Do not click the link or call the number in the message.
- Close the message or pop-up.
- Type the company's real address yourself, or call the number on your card or bill.
- If a pop-up will not close, turn off the device and ask someone you trust.
Words to know:
- Link: text you tap or click that takes you to a website.
- Pop-up: a box that suddenly appears on your screen.
- Phishing: a fake message that tries to get you to give away private information.
Official sources:
- Medicare: Reporting Medicare fraud and abuse
Try it now: On your safety card, write your bank's phone number copied from the back of your bank card, and your doctor's office number from a bill or appointment card. These are your trusted numbers.
You can now spot fake messages and pop-ups and reach companies safely using numbers you trust.

check.q: Why is perfect spelling no longer proof a message is real?
options: Banks never check spelling
AI helps scammers write messages with perfect spelling
All emails are checked by the government
Spelling does not matter in texts
check.why: AI writes clean, real-looking messages, so good spelling proves nothing.

check.q: An email says there is unusual activity on your bank account and to log in at a link. What do you do?
options: Click the link and log in
Reply with your password
Call the number in the email
Close it and type your bank's real address yourself, or call the number on your card
check.why: Links and numbers in unexpected messages lead to the scammer; reach the bank yourself.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: The Stop, Check, Call habit
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 4 minutes
Goal: Use three steps every time a message or call worries you.
This lesson builds toward: Every time a message or call worries you, you will use the Stop, Check, Call steps, using only a number you already trust.
Scammers win by rushing you. Your best defense is a habit you use every time: Stop, Check, Call.
Stop: do not click, pay, or give any information. It is fine to hang up on anyone, even if they say they are the police or the bank. Check: look for the four signs. Talk to someone you trust before you act. Call: contact the person or company yourself, using a number from your safety card, your bank card, a bill or the official website you typed in yourself.
You can also ask an AI assistant for a second opinion. Paste the message, after removing any private details, and ask: "Does this message show signs of a scam?" Treat its answer as a helper, not the final word; your Stop, Check, Call steps still come first.
Step by step:
- Stop: do not click, pay or share anything.
- Check: look for the four signs and talk to someone you trust.
- Call: use a number you already trust, never one from the message.
Words to know:
- Second opinion: asking someone else to look at something before you decide.
Try it now: Write Stop, Check, Call on your safety card. Then ask an AI assistant: "Does this message show signs of a scam? Your package is held. Pay $1.99 at this link today or it will be returned." Compare its answer with the four signs.
You can now use the Stop, Check, Call habit and ask AI for a careful second opinion.

check.q: In Stop, Check, Call, what does Call mean?
options: Call the number in the message
Call back the person who called you
Contact the person or company using a number you already trust
Call a friend to pay for you
check.why: Call means using a number from your safety card, bank card, a bill or a website you typed yourself.

check.q: A caller says he is from the police and you must not hang up. What can you do?
options: Hang up; it is fine to hang up on anyone
Stay on the line no matter what
Give him your address
Pay him to end the call
check.why: Stop means you can hang up on anyone, even someone who says they are the police.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Protecting your money and your information
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: List the details and payments you never give to an unexpected caller or message.
This lesson builds toward: When an unexpected caller or message asks for information or money, you will refuse to give private numbers, passwords, codes or unusual payments, and call your bank if you already did, sharing nothing with an unexpected contact.
Never give these to anyone who contacts you unexpectedly: your Social Security or Medicare number, bank or card numbers, passwords, or a code that was texted to your phone. Your bank already knows your account number; a real bank will not ask for your password or texted code.
Never pay a stranger with gift cards, wire transfers, cryptocurrency or a payment app, and never deposit a check and send part of the money back. The FTC says real government offices will never tell you to move money to "protect" it, withdraw cash, or buy gold.
Never let a caller connect to your computer to "fix" it. If you already gave money or information, act quickly: call your bank using the number on your card and tell it what happened.
Step by step:
- Never share Social Security, Medicare, bank or card numbers with an unexpected contact.
- Never share passwords or texted codes.
- Never pay strangers with gift cards, wires, crypto or payment apps.
- If you already paid or shared, call your bank right away using the number on your card.
Words to know:
- Texted code: a short number sent to your phone to prove it is really you signing in.
- Wire transfer: sending money electronically; it is very hard to get back.
Official sources:
- FTC: How to avoid a scam
Try it now: On your safety card, write: "I never share my numbers, passwords or codes with anyone who contacts me first. I never pay strangers with gift cards, wires or crypto."
You can now protect your private details and refuse risky payments.

check.q: What will a real bank never ask you for?
options: To visit a branch
Your password or a code texted to your phone
To read your statement
To call the number on your card
check.why: Your bank already knows your account; it will not ask for your password or texted code.

check.q: You realize you gave your card number to a scammer an hour ago. What do you do first?
options: Wait to see what happens
Call the scammer back
Post about it online
Call your bank right away using the number on your card
check.why: Acting quickly with your bank is the first step if you already shared money or information.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Reporting a scam and getting help
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Name where to report a scam and where to get support.
This lesson builds toward: After a scam or attempted scam, you will name where to report it and get help in the United States, naming at least two correct places.
Reporting helps stop scammers and can help you. In the United States, you can report scams to the Federal Trade Commission at ReportFraud.ftc.gov. Internet crimes can also be reported to the FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center at ic3.gov.
If you are 60 or older, the National Elder Fraud Hotline, run by the Department of Justice, is free: call 833-FRAUD-11 (833-372-8311). When we checked, it was open Monday to Friday, 10 am to 6 pm Eastern time, with help in English, Spanish and other languages. Check the hotline's website for current hours.
If someone uses your information, go to IdentityTheft.gov for a free recovery plan. If Medicare fraud is involved, call 1-800-MEDICARE (1-800-633-4227). Real reporting sites will never ask you to pay to get your money back; anyone who does is another scam.
Step by step:
- Call your bank first if money was taken.
- Report at ReportFraud.ftc.gov.
- Age 60 or older: call the Elder Fraud Hotline, 833-372-8311.
- If your identity was used: go to IdentityTheft.gov.
- Beware of anyone who charges to recover your money.
Words to know:
- Report: telling the right office what happened so it can act.
- Identity theft: when someone uses your personal information to pretend to be you.
Official sources:
- FTC: Report fraud
- DOJ Office for Victims of Crime: National Elder Fraud Hotline
- FBI Internet Crime Complaint Center
- FTC: What to know about identity theft
- Medicare: Reporting fraud and abuse
Try it now: Final task: finish your scam safety card. Add the places to report a scam and the Elder Fraud Hotline number. Then judge these two messages with the four signs: (1) "Hi Grandpa, new number, I'm in trouble, send $500 in gift cards"; (2) a reminder from your pharmacy that your prescription is ready, with no link and no request for money.
You can now spot a scam, check it safely, protect your money, and report it to the right place.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Trusted numbers and steps Fewer than three trusted numbers, or a number copied from a message. Three trusted numbers (family, bank from the back of the card, doctor's office) and the Stop, Check, Call steps written down. Can explain where each number came from and why it can be trusted. Family code word No family code word, or it is easy to guess or posted online. A family code word is written on the card and shared with family. Has practiced asking for it in a pretend emergency call. Places to report No places to report, or wrong ones. At least two correct places, such as ReportFraud.ftc.gov and the Elder Fraud Hotline. Also lists IdentityTheft.gov and says to call the bank first if money was taken. Sample messages judged Missed that a sample message was a scam. Judged both sample messages correctly and named the signs found. Said what they would do next, using Stop, Check, Call. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

options: A free recovery plan if someone uses your information
Buying identity insurance
Paying your taxes
Reporting a lost phone
check.why: IdentityTheft.gov gives a free recovery plan when your information is used.

check.q: A company calls offering to get your lost money back for a fee. What is this?
options: A government service
A normal refund
Probably another scam
A bank you can trust
check.why: Real reporting sites never ask you to pay to get your money back.
